transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-02 15:00 UTC | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Samir, Lena, Marcus (Redwood) — Alicia, Tom, Priya, Daniel (HelixCare)

Summary: Technical deep dive on integrating Redwood's runtime telemetry with HelixCare's OpenTelemetry pipeline. Focus on token-level metrics, trace/span strategy for per-token latency, KV cache hit/miss instrumentation, batching attribution, quantization observability, and constraints around VPC/on-prem collectors and PII.

Topics: OpenTelemetry export (OTLP/gRPC), token metrics vs request metrics, span strategy, histogram bucketing for latency pctiles, batching attribution labels, KV cache hit/miss counters, sampling strategy, cost of telemetry, dashboard templates, dedicated + on-prem considerations.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, I'm Samir with Redwood, AE on this account. we were joined today by Lena, our SE, and Marcus product. Alicia, Tom, thanks for setting the agenda.
[00:18] Alicia: Yeah thanks Samir, appreciated. We want to understand how to get token-level observability into our existing OTEL stack without blowing up our telemetry costs, and also how that works for Dedicated and our planned on-prem rollout.
[00:30] Lena: Great, yup we'll walk through the recommended approach. Quick note — some of the terminology in the transcript may be off, e.g., "Redwod" or "K-V cash" cropping up in auto transcribe, so please ignore.
[00:45] Tom: Haha yeah i've seen that. Ok start with the big picture, what's the minimum viable set of metrics we need to get meaningful insights for latency/cost trade-offs?
[00:58] Lena: Minimum viable: per-request metrics (requests/sec, success/error counts, 50/95/99 latency), and then token-level counters for tokens produced and tokens consumed, plus a small set of histograms for per-token latency. We also recommend labels for model, variant, route, and batch_size.
[01:17] Samir: To expand: token-level metrics are basically a counter incremented per output token and ideally a per-token latency histogram — that lets you slice cost per token, and p99 token latency when batching. Without that you only see request-level p99 which hides token tail behavior.
[01:34] Priya: How do we avoid cardinality explosion? If we tag by request_id or user_id that's going to kill our metrics backend.
[01:41] Lena: Exactly, don't tag with high-cardinality fields like request_id or user_id. Use labels: model_name, model_version, route, batch_size, cache_hit boolean, quantization_profile. Keep label values bounded — e.g. bucket batch_size into categories: small/medium/large.
[02:04] Daniel: And for traces — do we instrument every token as a span or do we aggregate?
[02:10] Marcus: Good question. We recommend aggregated spans: one parent span per request with child attributes summarizing token phases, and optionally emit a single representative per-token span for slow tokens (above threshold) to keep trace volume manageable. Instrumentation pattern: request span -> child span for decode loop with attributes token_count, kv_cache_hits, batch_contrib. If you need debugging you can turn on per-token spans in staging only.
[02:36] Alicia: Can you walk through how KV cache hit/miss gets surfaced? We'd like to correlate KV misses with latency spikes.
[02:42] Lena: We emit two counters: kv_cache_hit{model,route} and kv_cache_miss{...}. Also a gauge for kv_cache_hit_rate as a percentage. For traces we add attributes to the decode span: kv_hits, kv_misses, kv_latency_ms. Then in Grafana you can pivot p95 latency by kv_cache_miss > 0.
[03:00] Tom: Are those counters emitted from the runtime itself or from the collector side?
[03:05] Lena: Runtime emits metrics to an OTLP exporter inside Redwood Private or Dedicated — on Hosted we push aggregated metrics to Redwood monitoring and expose OTEL-compatible endpoints. For Private/VPC we recommend running an OTEL Collector in the same VPC, configured to receive OTLP/gRPC from the runtime and forward to your backend (Prometheus, Cortex, Datadog).
[03:27] Priya: Any sample configs? We've got strict egress controls for our on-prem setup.
[03:32] Samir: We'll share a sample OTLP collector config — enclosed in the next steps. For egress-constrained environments you can point the collector at your internal telemetry endpoint and disable remote exporters.
[03:45] Alicia: How do we handle PII in traces and logs? We need to ensure no user PII is sent in spans for compliance.
[03:52] Daniel: This is huge for us.
[03:55] Lena: Runtime will not emit request bodies by default. Attributes are high-level stats (token counts, cache hits, model ids). If you enable debug-level spans, you must use filters to redact prompt text. We provide a config flag to obfuscate or hash prompt identifiers before export.
[04:12] Marcus: Also audit logging for Private includes hashes of requests rather than raw text and an option to keep logs locally only. We'll include the KMS key rotation notes in the security doc.
[04:24] Tom: Back to token-level histograms — what bucketization do you recommend?
[04:29] Lena: Use exponential buckets for token latency (e.g., 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 ms) depending on your model/hardware. For request-level latency use ms buckets up to a couple seconds. The important bit is measuring per-token p99.
[04:46] Priya: If we enable token metrics at production scale, what’s the cost implication? A rough order of magnitude?
[04:52] Samir: It depends on retention and where you store metrics. Token counters are low-cost; histograms and traces are heavier. If you sample traces 1% and keep histograms at 30d, typical telemetry cost bump is low-mid single-digit percent for telemetry ingestion but could be material for hosted SaaS backends — we can provide an estimate after seeing HelixCare's traffic profile.
[05:15] Alicia: We want a dashboard that correlates model variant, batch size, kv_hit_rate, and p99 token latency. Can you show an example query?
[05:22] Lena: Sure — for Prometheus: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(token_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, model_variant, batch_category, cache_hit)). For KV correlation you can do a join on kv_cache_miss rate and latency. We'll share the dashboard JSON.
[05:40] Tom: About batching — how does Redwood attribute latency to batch composition when requests are multiplexed into the same batch?
[05:47] Marcus: We emit a batch_id label on metrics for debugging, but avoid it in prod because of cardinality. Instead we emit batch_size and batch_position buckets (first/middle/last) and also the per-request contribution time: per_request_enqueue_ms and per_request_dequeue_ms which help you see whether requests that arrived late in a batch see additional latency.
[06:10] Priya: For quantization and perf — can telemetry show which quantization profile was used for a given request?
[06:16] Lena: Yes include quant_profile label in request metrics. For traces add quant_profile and quant_inference_ms attribute so you can compare quantized vs full precision latency and CPU/GPU utilization.
[06:28] Daniel: On the private deployment side, how do we run the OTEL collector inside our air-gapped environment? Any special packaging?
[06:35] Samir: We provide an on-prem collector bundle that runs as a service inside the VPC or air-gapped cluster. It supports file-based exporters if you need to bundle and ship. For fully air-gapped we can enable local retention and a manual export path. We'll include these options in the security pack.
[06:51] Alicia: Can you talk about sampling strategy for traces so we still detect tail latency issues?
[06:56] Marcus: Use adaptive sampling: baseline 0.5-1% sampling, with rule-based overrides to capture all traces with token latency > X ms or requests with KV misses > 0. That keeps ingest low but ensures you capture problematic flows.
[07:12] Tom: Is there a simple way to correlate infra-level GPU metrics with per-token latency?
[07:17] Lena: Yes, tag your GPU utilization metrics with model_name and host_id and use a dashboard that overlays GPU utilization + token p95/p99. For deeper correlation we also emit metrics for kv cache latency and batch fill rate so you can see if latency is due to compute saturation or batching inefficiencies.
[07:36] Priya: A nit — our metrics team is on Cortex/Thanos stack. Any special concerns?
[07:41] Samir: Thanos/Cortex is fine. Prometheus histograms work as usual. Watch cardinality and use relabel_configs in the OTEL Collector to drop high-cardinality labels. We'll include example relabel rules in the config bundle.
[07:58] Alicia: Can you run through a small end-to-end example — request arrives, goes through KV cache, batching, decode, and what telemetry gets emitted at each stage?
[08:08] Lena: Sure: 1) Ingest: increment request_received counter with labels model/route; 2) Preprocess: emit attribute preprocess_ms; 3) KV lookup: increment kv_cache_hit/miss counters and add kv_latency_ms attribute; 4) Batching: emit batch_enqueue_ms, batch_size label, batch_position; 5) Decode: increment token_counter per token, observe token_latency histogram per token; 6) Finish: request_duration histogram, request_success counter and sample trace with decode attributes.
[08:45] Tom: Sounds good. One more thing: for Hosted Redwood customers do you provide direct OTLP exports so we can pull metrics into our Datadog?
[08:53] Samir: Hosted customers can use Redwood's export bridge; we can forward OTLP -> Datadog, or export Prometheus metrics for scraping. For enterprise Dedicated/Private you get full OTLP endpoints you control.
[09:05] Priya: Are there any known pitfalls when instrumenting quantized runtimes for metrics?
[09:10] Lena: Watch for mismatch between token latency attribution and GPU kernel batching specifics — sometimes per-token timings look better in CPU wall-clock but kernel launch overheads cause spikes. We recommend capturing both host-level and runtime-level timings and correlating them. Also ensure quant_profile label is applied consistently across variants.
[09:28] Marcus: Also be careful about double-counting tokens when caching prefixes — ensure your token_counter only increments for newly emitted tokens, not for replaying cached prefixes. We'll include a note in the instrumentation guide, because transcribers sometimes show "KV cache double count" as a reported issue.
[09:46] Alicia: This is really helpful. For the benchmark run you mentioned — what do you need from us to run a representative test?
[09:52] Samir: A sample traffic profile CSV with request rates, prompt length distribution, and model/version. Also desired SLAs (p95 < X ms), and whether we should test with KV cache warm and cold.
[10:03] Alicia: We'll prepare and share.
[10:06] Tom: Any limitations on the OTEL SDK versions we should be aware of?
[10:11] Lena: We currently validate against otel v1.x stable series and recommend using OTLP/gRPC, not HTTP/proto. Collector version guidance will be in the config bundle.
[10:21] Daniel: Security — will the collector or runtime attempt to phone home? Need to highlight that for our security review.
[10:27] Samir: For Private we don't phone home by default — only the control plane during registration if you opt in. The telemetry exporter can be locked to internal endpoints; we document flags to disable external endpoints.
[10:40] Priya: Great. Anything else we should keep in mind for dashboards?
[10:44] Lena: Two dashboard types: 1) SLO ops dashboard with p50/p95/p99 latency, error rates, kv_hit_rate, tokens/sec; 2) cost/perf dashboard with token-cost estimates, model-cost per 1k tokens, batch efficiency. We'll provide templates for Grafana.
[11:02] Alicia: Okay let's recap next steps.
[11:05] Samir: Recap: Samir sends OTEL integration notes + sample collector config; Lena shares Prometheus/Grafana dashboard JSON and example queries; HelixCare shares traffic profile; Redwood runs benchmark on Dedicated and returns results; schedule follow up 2026-12-09.
[11:23] Tom: Thanks everyone.
[11:25] Priya: Thanks, bye.
[11:27] Marcus: Bye all.

Post-call notes:

- Recommended sampling policy: 1% baseline + rule to capture traces with kv_miss > 0 or token_latency > 50 ms.
